name: Marxism
summary: Marxism is the body of thought that begins with Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. It holds that history is driven by class struggle rooted in how production is organised, that capitalism rests on the exploitation of wage labour, and that the working class must take political power and replace private ownership of the means of production with common ownership and production for need. Through a transitional proletarian state it aims at a classless, stateless society without wage labour, in which distribution follows need.
scope: The theory of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, as the Marxists Internet Archive's glossary says the name 'originates from the political and scientific work of Karl Marx and Frederick Engels in the 1840s' and as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy sets out Marx's thought: the Manifesto and the Principles of Communism, the Critique of the Gotha Programme, The Civil War in France, the International's instructions Marx drafted, and Engels' Anti-Duhring and Origin of the Family. Later uses of the word (Leninist, social-democratic, council and other strands, and the regimes that called themselves Marxist) are other subjects here, so their records and texts are not used; where the founders' own texts are silent the answer is null.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Credit is to be centralised in the hands of the state, the opposite of leaving money to the market.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Marx's higher phase of communism comes after the enslaving subordination to the division of labour has vanished.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Manifesto attacks feudal and aristocratic privilege and demands abolition of all right of inheritance.

abolish-income-tax.rationale: The second measure of the Manifesto is 'a heavy progressive or graduated income tax'.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Principles of Communism says that once all capital, production and exchange are in the hands of the nation, 'private property will disappear of its own accord, money will become superfluous'.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: The Manifesto says 'there can no longer be any wage-labour when there is no longer any capital', and the Gotha critique calls the wage system 'a system of slavery' to be abolished.

alienated-labor.rationale: Marx's theory of alienation holds that wage labour under capitalism separates workers from their product, their activity and each other.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: The Manifesto's first measure is 'abolition of property in land and application of all rents of land to public purposes', and Principles of Communism has landowners gradually expropriated and land publicly owned.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Marx defended freedom of conscience and, in the Commune, disestablished the church; punishing leaving a religion is opposed to this.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Principles of Communism says communists know that 'all conspiracies are not only useless, but even harmful' and that revolutions 'are not made intentionally and arbitrarily' but follow from conditions independent of the will of parties.

bound-labor.rationale: Serfdom is a historical form of class exploitation to be abolished.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Marx held that capitalism's recurring crises drive it toward overthrow.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The Manifesto praises the bourgeoisie for creating immense productive forces and laying the material basis for communism.

central-bank-independence.rationale: The Manifesto puts credit under a national bank with state capital and an exclusive monopoly, a bank controlled by the state rather than independent of it.

central-planning.rationale: Production is to be consciously and cooperatively regulated, though Marx refused to draw up blueprints.

character-from-environment.rationale: The Manifesto holds that people's ideas and consciousness change with their material conditions.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Marx held that the Commune aimed at "the disestablishment and disendowment of all churches as proprietary bodies".

class-collaboration.rationale: Class antagonism is irreconcilable under capitalism.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The Manifesto opens with the claim that all history is the history of class struggles.

clerical-rule.rationale: Marx held religion to be ideology and wanted priests "sent back to the recesses of private life", so clerical authority is opposed.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The instructions Marx drafted say unions arose to win better terms of contract from capital on 'questions of wages and time of labour', an activity that must be generalised across countries.

collective-farming.rationale: Engels' Principles of Communism holds that agriculture is held back by the 'division of privately owned land into small parcels', and the Manifesto's measures bring land under a common plan with industrial armies 'especially for agriculture'.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: History is driven by class struggle, but the aim is to end competitive class society for cooperative common ownership.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Marx's sketch of the Commune's national organisation has rural communities send delegates to district assemblies, which send deputies to a national delegation, each 'revocable and bound by the mandat imperatif', with the few remaining central functions discharged by communal agents; his 1852 stress on 'centralisation' was an earlier position.

conscription.rationale: The instructions Marx drafted propose the general armament of the people and general instruction in the use of arms, with small standing armies in which 'every male citizen' serves for a very limited time.

cooperative-communities.rationale: The Manifesto's critique of critical-utopian socialism dismisses founding isolated 'phalansteres', 'Home Colonies' or a 'Little Icaria' as 'castles in the air' that sink into reaction.

corporate-influence.rationale: The Manifesto calls the modern state a committee for managing the bourgeoisie's common affairs.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Marx described barbarian nations drawn into civilisation by the bourgeoisie and ranked societies by stage of production.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: The instructions Marx drafted recommend 'the total abolition of indirect taxes' and their replacement by direct taxes, which covers exempting necessities from consumption taxes.

defeat-communism.rationale: Communism is the Marxist goal, so treating it as a threat to be defeated is the opposite of its position.

delink-world-market.rationale: Marx treated free trade as hastening capitalism's contradictions, not as a reason to withdraw.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Part IV of the Critique of the Gotha Programme says the political transition between capitalist and communist society needs a state that 'can be nothing but the revolutionary dictatorship of the proletariat'.

distribute-by-need.rationale: From each according to ability, to each according to needs is Marx's formula for the higher phase.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Marx treats religion as a product of social conditions and holds that political power is class power, not divinely given.

elective-rulers.rationale: In the Commune, officials were elected and revocable, which Marx praised, and he opposed hereditary rule.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The Manifesto's programme calls for a heavy progressive or graduated income tax.

free-public-college.rationale: In the Critique of the Gotha Programme (part IV) Marx says "free" higher education "only means in fact defraying the cost of education of the upper classes from the general tax receipts"; he says this of class society, and later Marxists often back free tuition.

free-trade.rationale: Marx described free trade as the single unconscionable freedom of the bourgeoisie, though he saw it as hastening revolution.

gradual-change.rationale: The Manifesto expects the bourgeoisie to be overthrown by force rather than reformed piecemeal.

harm-principle.rationale: Marx held that liberal rights protect individuals from one another and leave inequality intact.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The Gotha critique and Manifesto treat labour as the source of wealth and propose rewards by contribution of labour, attacking the idle owners of capital.

indirect-election.rationale: In Marx's account of the Commune's plan, district assemblies of delegates send deputies to the national delegation, so officials at higher levels are chosen through delegates from the communes.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Marx criticised the liberal rights of egoistic individuals and stressed class and community.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Marx did not romanticise pre-industrial life and saw industry as part of the solution.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: The Manifesto's remedy for credit is its centralisation in a state bank, not user-owned mutual banks.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Capital builds on the claim that the value of commodities is set by the socially necessary labour that produces them, and the Gotha critique says labour is the source of all wealth and culture only when it is social.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Religion is ideology, and law follows material relations.

legal-duty-to-work.rationale: The Manifesto's measures for advanced countries include 'Equal liability of all to work' with industrial armies, repeated in Principles of Communism as 'an equal obligation on all members of society to work'.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The Manifesto calls for centralising credit, transport and communication in public hands, and common ownership generally.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Marx held that commodity production and market exchange generate exploitation and crises, and looked to conscious social regulation of production.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Historical materialism, that the mode of production shapes political and intellectual life, is the core of Marxist theory.

means-match-ends.rationale: Marx accepted a coercive revolutionary dictatorship as a transitional means to a stateless end.

moral-incentives.rationale: The Critique of the Gotha Programme looks to a higher phase in which labour becomes life's prime want and distribution is by need, not material reward.

more-religion-public.rationale: Religion is the opium of the people, an illusion that fades when material life is emancipated.

municipal-property.rationale: Marx wanted the means of production held in common by society as a whole, not by localities or private owners.

nation-first.rationale: Workers have no country and class solidarity crosses borders.

national-church-status.rationale: Marx held that the Commune disestablished the church; privileged state religion is rejected.

national-self-determination.rationale: The instructions Marx drafted for the International name 'the right of nations to self-determination' as the means of restoring a democratic Poland and ending Russian influence, but they apply it to cases chosen for their effect on the workers' cause rather than to every people.

native-born-offices.rationale: The Manifesto says workers have no country and calls for the abolition of nationality as a basis for rights.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Marxism holds communism is the sound successor to capitalism, so a third course is rejected.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The Manifesto holds that the bourgeois state serves property, and calls for the abolition of private property and state control of credit, transport and industry.

no-central-bank.rationale: The Manifesto and Principles of Communism call for centralising credit in the hands of the state 'by means of a national bank with State capital and an exclusive monopoly' and suppressing private banks.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Engels says that where affection ends 'separation is a benefit for both partners as well as for society', sparing people 'the useless mire of a divorce case'.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Marx praises the Commune for opening all schools to the people free and 'cleared of all interference of church and state', and in the Gotha critique says government and church should be 'equally excluded from any influence on the school'.

no-transition-to-communism.rationale: Marx holds that between capitalist and communist society lies a period of revolutionary transformation whose state 'can be nothing but the revolutionary dictatorship of the proletariat', which he calls a transition to the abolition of classes.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: Marx told the 1872 Hague congress that in America, England and perhaps Holland workers 'can attain their goal by peaceful means', and Engels in 1895 says the 'revolutionists' thrive better with legal means than illegal ones.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Marx praised the Commune as democracy without professionals, with delegates recallable and officials paid a worker's wage, and communism aims at associated producers governing their own work.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The Manifesto describes the bourgeois family as treating women as mere instruments of production, and Marxism links gender hierarchy to class society.

people-in-arms.rationale: The instructions Marx drafted propose 'the general armament of the people' and accept small standing armies only as a 'transitory necessity', and he praises the Commune for replacing the standing army with the armed people.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The Manifesto abolishes bourgeois property in the means of production while leaving personal possessions earned by labour, and the Gotha Programme calls for common ownership of the means of production.

physical-labour-duty.rationale: The instructions Marx drafted hold that no able-bodied adult should be exempt from the law of nature 'to work in order to be able to eat', and work 'not only with the brain but with the hands too'.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Marx attacks Lassalle's iron law as resting on 'the Malthusian theory of population' and scorns the claim that poverty 'has its basis in nature'; he ties poverty to wage labour and capitalist production.

positive-liberty.rationale: Marx held real freedom needs material conditions and communal emancipation, beyond mere political rights.

premarital-sex.rationale: Principles of Communism says communist society will make relations between the sexes 'a purely private matter which concerns only the persons involved and into which society has no occasion to intervene'.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The Manifesto says workers have no country and expects national distinctions to fade.

production-for-use.rationale: Principles of Communism has society operate all branches of production 'for the common account, according to a common plan' so that the needs of all are met, in place of competing private producers.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Profit derives from surplus value, labour beyond that needed to reproduce workers.

property-franchise.rationale: The Manifesto calls the proletarian movement that of the immense majority, and the Commune rested on universal suffrage, so a wealth test contradicts it.

property-fundamental.rationale: The communists' aim is summed up as abolition of private property, with despotic inroads on its rights.

public-money-creation.rationale: The Manifesto's ten measures include centralising credit in the hands of the state through a national bank.

public-ownership.rationale: The Manifesto's measures include state-owned factories and state control of credit and transport.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Marx claimed a scientific outlook and treated religion as illusion.

recall-officials.rationale: Marx wrote that Commune councillors and delegates were "responsible and revocable at short terms".

recallable-delegates.rationale: The Commune's delegates were bound by their electors and revocable at any time, which Marx praised as the model of proletarian rule.

reification.rationale: Commodity fetishism, in which social relations between people appear as relations between things, is a core Marxian idea.

religion-illusion.rationale: Marx called religion the opium of the people and the sigh of the oppressed creature, and expected it to fade as conditions changed.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Marx and Engels say communism abolishes all religion and eternal truths, and treat religion as a product of class society, not a shared truth.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Marx praised the Paris Commune, where "the public service had to be done at workman's wage" from its members downward.

restore-past-order.rationale: Marx saw the past as nothing to restore and looked forward to a new society.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The International's instructions describe trade-union activity on wages and hours as 'legitimate' and 'necessary' and urge that it be generalised, so a law restricting strikes runs against the stated position.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Marx held industry and technology make human liberation possible.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The Manifesto says the bourgeoisie rescued a considerable part of the population from the idiocy of rural life.

separate-church-state.rationale: Marx saw political emancipation from religion as a real if insufficient advance.

separated-powers.rationale: Marx praises the Commune because it was 'a working, not a parliamentary body, executive and legislative at the same time', the opposite of dividing power among bodies that check one another.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Marx held that human nature is shaped by history and social relations rather than fixed, though he also wrote of species-being; adherents are divided.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Manifesto attacks the bourgeois family as built on private property and Engels held that monogamous marriage rested on the subjection of women.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The 1872 Preface to the Manifesto says the Commune proved that 'the working class cannot simply lay hold of the ready-made state machinery, and wield it for its own purposes'.

social-market-economy.rationale: Principles of Communism says bourgeois socialists, who want to keep present society and only remove its evils through 'mere welfare measures' or reform systems, must be struggled against 'unremittingly' by communists.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The Manifesto makes the proletariat's winning of political power the means of socialism, so state ownership without workers in power is not socialism.

socialism-one-country.rationale: The Manifesto says 'united action, of the leading civilised countries at least, is one of the first conditions for the emancipation of the proletariat', and Engels answers 'No' to whether the revolution can happen in one country alone.

socialized-care.rationale: The Manifesto calls for replacing home education by social education and abolishing the bourgeois family, and Engels argued for socialising domestic work, though Marx gave few details.

socialized-markets.rationale: Engels' Principles of Communism says the new order must 'abolish competition and replace it with association', with production run by society as a whole for the common account; a market economy of worker-owned firms keeps the competition and separate accounts it rejects.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Political power is the organised power of one class for oppressing another.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The Manifesto centralises credit and extends state-owned instruments of production.

state-finances-worker-businesses.rationale: Marx mocks the Gotha programme's call for producers' co-operatives set up 'with state aid', saying a new society cannot be built with state loans 'just as well as a new railway' and that it must arise from the revolutionary transformation of society.

state-harmful.rationale: Engels writes that the proletariat in power 'abolishes also the state as state', and the Manifesto says the public power loses its political character once class distinctions disappear; a transitional proletarian state comes first (Gotha critique, part IV), so the abolition is the stated end, not an immediate act.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Abolition of all right of inheritance is a Manifesto measure.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: A heavy progressive income tax is the second of the Manifesto's measures for advanced countries.

taxation-theft.rationale: The Manifesto itself proposes heavy progressive taxation.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Hostility between nations is expected to end with class antagonisms.

total-state.rationale: The state is expected to wither away, and the aim is free development of each.

traditional-family.rationale: The Manifesto holds the bourgeois family rests on capital and private gain and will vanish with it; Engels' Origins treats monogamous marriage as male domination.

unions-good.rationale: Marx's instructions for the International call trade-union action over wages and working time 'not only legitimate' but 'necessary' while capital lasts, and say unions must generalise and go on to act as organising centres for the class's emancipation, not stop at local wage fights.

universal-morality.rationale: Moral ideas are held to be historical and class-conditioned.

unpaid-domestic-work-exploitation.rationale: Engels writes that the modern individual family 'is founded on the open or concealed domestic slavery of the wife' and that within it 'the husband is the bourgeois and the wife represents the proletariat'.

wages-fall-to-bare-minimum.rationale: The Manifesto and Principles of Communism say the wage sinks to the minimum needed to live, but in the Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875) Marx rejects Lassalle's 'iron law' as a false formulation resting on Malthus, and says wages are the price of labour power; the earlier statement was replaced.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The Manifesto holds industry is already destroying small property and aims at common ownership.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Marx told the 1872 Hague congress that abstention from political action is 'dangerous and fatal' and that the worker must some day seize political power, like the old Christians who despised politics and lost 'Heaven on Earth'.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Manifesto ties the family and the position of women to bourgeois property relations and calls for their abolition, and Engels developed this link.

worker-farmer-alliance.rationale: Principles of Communism says that in America communists must make common cause with the agrarian National Reformers, and that in France and Germany the small peasants are increasingly dependent on the proletariat's political interests.

worker-ownership.rationale: Marx envisaged production on the basis of common ownership of the means of production, usually by the associated producers society-wide rather than firm by firm.

workers-councils.rationale: Marx praises the Paris Commune as 'a working, not a parliamentary body, executive and legislative at the same time' and as the political form at last discovered for the economic emancipation of labour.

workers-nation.rationale: The Manifesto: the working men have no country.

workers-own-party.rationale: The 1850 Address of the Central Committee urges that the workers' party go into battle 'with the maximum degree of organization, unity and independence' so that it is not taken in tow by the bourgeoisie or petty-bourgeois democrats, and Marx told the Hague congress the working class must fight on political as well as social grounds.

workers-parties-campaign-reforms.rationale: The Manifesto says the communists 'fight for the attainment of the immediate aims, for the enforcement of the momentary interests of the working class', and Marx's instructions for the International demand a legal eight-hour day.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Collective control of production by the associated producers is the aim.

missingStatements.text: The state is essentially a tool by which the ruling class dominates the others.
missingStatements.rationale: The Manifesto defines political power as the organised power of one class for oppressing another and the modern state as a committee managing the bourgeoisie's common affairs.

missingStatements.text: Education should be combined with productive work.
missingStatements.rationale: The Manifesto's tenth measure and Engels' Principles of Communism both pair public education with production, to free children from the one-sided division of labour.

quotes.text: Combination of education with industrial production

missingStatements.text: The rural-urban divide should be abolished.
missingStatements.rationale: The Manifesto lists the gradual abolition of the distinction between town and country as a measure, and Principles of Communism says the difference is destined to disappear under communal production.

quotes.text: gradual abolition of all the distinction between town and country
the difference between city and country is destined to disappear

notes: Rules-7 later pass (2026-11-13) on an audit written under no rules version. Every earlier answer was checked against Marx and Engels' own texts, saved in scratchpad/sources/marxism/ (Manifesto chapters 1-4 and the 1872 preface, Principles of Communism, Gotha critique parts I-IV, Civil War in France, the International's 1866 instructions, the 1850 Address, the 1872 Hague speech, the 1852 Weydemeyer letter, Anti-Duhring, Origin of the Family, Engels' 1895 Introduction). Answers that rested only on Wikipedia, on later Marxists disagreeing, or on an inference were nulled (reviewHistory); several others were re-sourced to the texts. Themes searched: wages and unions, the working day, taxation and credit, state and transition, the Commune's political forms, religion and schools, family and women, nationality and colonies, war and armies, revolution versus legal means, property, money and planning. Nothing is answered from Marxism-Leninism or later strands. No text was found in which Marx or Engels addresses modern issues such as immigration levels, nuclear power, drugs, gun control or AI, so those are null.

keyFigures.role: Principal founder of the theory, author of Capital and co-author of the Manifesto.
keyFigures.quote: It originates from the political and scientific work of Karl Marx and Frederick Engels in the 1840s

keyFigures.role: Co-founder; co-author of the Manifesto and author of Principles of Communism, Anti-Duhring and The Origin of the Family.
keyFigures.quote: It originates from the political and scientific work of Karl Marx and Frederick Engels in the 1840s
